claims.text: Sub-critical annealing can produce finely dispersed nanoscale precipitates in magnetic high-entropy alloys.
Finely dispersed nanoscale precipitates increase coercive field by enhancing domain-wall pinning.
The initial material is an as-cast, multiphase magnetic high-entropy alloy with no post-processing heat treatment.
Controlled sub-critical annealing under an inert atmosphere induces nanoscale precipitate formation while avoiding full recrystallization.
The annealing treatment is performed below the recrystallization temperature with controlled duration and cooling conditions.
The proposed effect is particularly applicable to alloys with significant magnetic anisotropy and inherent microstructural heterogeneities.
Nanoscale precipitates formed during annealing act as pinning sites for magnetic domain walls.
Additional domain-wall pinning centers hinder magnetization reversal.
Hindering magnetization reversal increases the coercive field.
Sub-critical annealing will produce a statistically significant increase in coercive field relative to the as-cast baseline.
Preventing grain growth or recrystallization is necessary for the expected coercivity increase.
Alloys with very fine initial microstructures may show a reduced or ambiguous coercivity response.
Alloys with weak magnetic anisotropy may show a reduced or ambiguous coercivity response.
The magnitude of the coercive-field increase depends on alloy composition and annealing conditions.
